analysis.one_liner: Makes tobacco companies pay escalating fees unless youth use of their products drops sharply.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Commerce Committee and died when the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Health and Human Services Department to survey each year how many children under 18 used each tobacco company's products. Each company would have had to cut that number by 20% of its starting level the second year, then by 40%, 60%, 80%, and finally down to 10% of baseline by the sixth year. A company that missed its target would pay a fee of $1 per pack (or equivalent unit) sold, rising $1 for each consecutive year of failure, with the first $1 billion a year going into an enforcement and education fund. The bill never received a committee hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Children, by giving every tobacco company a direct financial reason to make sure fewer kids use its products, since the fee is charged per unit sold when youth targets are missed. The public also gains a dedicated fund for enforcement and anti-smoking education, and the bill explicitly leaves state and local tobacco laws untouched.

how_it_helps.text: Each manufacturer must reduce the number of children using its products by stages — 80% of baseline by year two, down to 10% of baseline by year six, or no more than a de minimis level of 0.5% of all child tobacco users [S3].

A manufacturer that misses a performance standard pays a $1 fee per unit distributed, rising by $1 for each consecutive year of violation, giving the company a direct financial stake in youth use rates [S3].
The first $1 billion of annual fees funds federal tobacco enforcement and public education to discourage children from smoking [S3].
The bill does not preempt any federal, state, or local law that reduces youth tobacco use, so stricter state rules would remain in place [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers, who would pay per-unit fees whenever children keep using their products; the costs could be passed to consumers through higher prices. Companies would also bear the cost of compliance testing against annual youth-use surveys.

drawbacks.text: The enforcement mechanism depends on annual surveys estimating how many children used each specific company's products, an indirect way to regulate that invites disputes over survey accuracy — judicial review is allowed only after fees are paid and only on an 'arbitrary and capricious' standard [S3].
The per-unit fee applies to all units sold when a target is missed, so costs would likely reach adult consumers through higher prices, not just the companies' youth marketing [S3].

Companies that come close to their targets get a proportional discount — 10% off the fee for each percentage point of the required reduction achieved above 90% — softening the penalty near the finish line [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill ties a large public health goal — driving child tobacco use down 90% within six years — to a self-funding penalty system, which is a genuinely strong design for its purpose. Its weaknesses are procedural rather than substantive: regulation by survey is indirect and contestable, near-compliance discounts give companies room to stall, and the bill leaves advertising and marketing untouched, the tools companies most directly control. On balance the benefits to children's health outweigh the costs, which fall mainly on an industry whose product is the leading preventable cause of death.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 1997 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the bill for himself and Sen. Lautenberg on June 3, 1997, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S3][S5].
The full action history shows only an introduction, introductory remarks, and the committee referral — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action was ever recorded [S5].
Durbin delivered additional introductory remarks on the bill in March 1998, but the bill remained parked in committee through the end of the Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers came out ahead: they never faced the per-unit penalties for youth use or the survey-based accountability the bill would have imposed, and no similar performance-standard law was enacted in that Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco manufacturers, which faced no penalties

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it twice, in June 1997 and March 1998 [S1][S5].

for.name: Sen. Frank Lautenberg
for.what_they_did: Joined Durbin in introducing the bill [S3].

against.name: John McCain
against.role: Chair, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill; it sat in committee from June 1997 until the Congress ended [S5].

against.name: Tobacco industry
against.role: Major lobbying presence in the 105th Congress
against.what_they_did: The industry mounted a well-documented lobbying campaign against tobacco-control legislation during the 1997-1998 settlement debates, a context widely reported at the time.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors and both cosponsors were Democrats; the bill died in a committee chaired by a Republican with no recorded Republican support [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have charged each company $1 per unit sold, escalating yearly, whenever children kept using its products, directly attacking the youth market that sustains future customer bases. Its interest ran against the bill's public-health goal.
The fee is levied on manufacturers, but costs would likely be passed through to prices, which could slightly reduce sales. The bill imposes no direct restrictions on retailers.
